## Logging in to greatlakes

We follow the [greatlakes user guide for getting started with the command line](https://documentation.its.umich.edu/node/5013). As preliminaries, you need:

- A Slurm account. You should already have a primary account, `stats_dept1`, and a smaller backup account for if you exhaust your resources, `stats_dept2`.

- A greatlakes cluster login account. If you have not yet filled in the form at <https://its.umich.edu/advanced-research-computing/high-performance-computing/great-lakes/getting-started> then do so.

- A umich internet address. Use the umich VPN if you are not on campus.


## Connecting to greatlakes with macOS, Linux or Windows

Use the umich VPN if you are not on campus.

1. Open a Terminal window and type

```bash
ssh uniqname@greatlakes.arc-ts.umich.edu
```

  where `uniqname` is your uniqname.

2. Login with your Kerberos level-1 password, and Duo two-factor authentication.

This creates a remote terminal shell on greatlakes.


## Connecting to greatlakes with a browser

Use the umich VPN if you are not on campus.

1. Point your browser to <https://greatlakes.arc-ts.umich.edu>

2. Choose the menu option: Clusters $\rightarrow$ Great Lakes Shell Access

This creates a remote terminal shell on greatlakes within your browser.


## Moving files on and off greatlakes using `scp`

On Mac or Linux, you can use `scp` which has similar syntax to `cp`.
To copy `myfile` on your laptop to a subdirectory `mydir` of your home directory on greatlakes:

```bash
scp myfile uniqname@greatlakes-xfer.arc-ts.umich.edu:mydir
```

To copy an entire directory, use the `-r` flag for recursive copy:

```bash
scp -r mydir uniqname@greatlakes-xfer.arc-ts.umich.edu:
```

These commands can also be reversed to copy files from greatlakes to your machine. The following copies `mydir` back to the current working directory:

```bash
scp -r uniqname@greatlakes-xfer.arc-ts.umich.edu:mydir .
```

You will need to authenticate via Duo to complete the file transfer.
On Mac or Windows, [FileZilla](https://filezilla-project.org) provides a file system user interface.


## Working with batch jobs

1. You create a batch script and submit it as a job
2. Your job is scheduled, and it enters the queue
3. When its turn arrives, your job will execute the batch script
4. Your script has access to all applications and data
5. When your script completes, anything it sent to standard output and error are saved in files stored in your submission directory
6. You can ask that email be sent to you when your jobs starts, ends, or fails
7. You can check on the status of your job at any time, or delete it if it's not doing what you want
8. A short time after your job completes, it disappears


## Useful batch commands

Submit a job
```bash
sbatch sample.sbat
```

Query job status
```bash
squeue -j jobid
squeue -u uniqname
```

Delete a job
```bash
scancel jobid
```

Check a job script and estimate its start time
```bash
sbatch --test-only sample.sbat
```

\begin{tabular}{ll}

\\
\texttt{seff jobid} & show cpu utilization for jobid
\\
\texttt{my\_accounts} & show all billing accounts on which you can run jobs
\end{tabular}

All Stats PhD students should have access to the `stats_dept1` and `stats_dept2` accounts.


## Python modules on greatlakes

Software on greatlakes is packaged in modules which must be loaded

```bash
module load python
```

Other versions of Python are available:

```bash
module avail python
```

The default module is appropriate for simple multicore computing. Check that it provides the packages we need:

```bash
python -c "import numpy, joblib"
```

Additional packages can be installed using `pip` at a terminal on the login node.


## Use a virtual environment

To avoid conflicts, it is good practice to create a virtual environment in your home directory:

```bash
python -m venv ~/myenv
source ~/myenv/bin/activate
pip install numpy joblib
```

Your home directory files (and therefore these packages) are accessible on all nodes of the cluster. If you use a virtual environment, activate it in your batch script.


## A test of `joblib`

- The `gl` subdirectory of the `810f26` git repo contains `test.sbat` that submits a batch job running the parallel `joblib` test in `test.py`.

- You can transfer the files from your laptop via `scp`, or by copy-paste.
  Or simply clone the class git repository into your greatlakes account,

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ionides/810f26.git
```

- Inspect the text file `test.sbat`, for example by

```bash
more test.sbat
```

- One thing that needs changing is to set your email address for alerts about jobs beginning and ending. To make these edits on greatlakes, you need a text editor. Options include

```bash
vi test.sbat
nano test.sbat
```

<!--
- It is useful to have basic familiarity with these editors, and you can ask the internet for help.
-->

## Comparing results

- You are now ready to run a batch job

```bash
sbatch test.sbat
```

- From inspecting the code in `test.py`, we see that the results are saved in `test.csv`

- Compare the run times with the results from running this code on your laptop, which you can do by `python test.py`.

- Also, try running the code in `test2.py` by

```bash
sbatch test2.sbat
```

  What do you learn from comparing the outputs in `test2.csv` with `test.csv` on greatlakes and your laptop?


## Other ways to run Python on greatlakes

- It is sometimes useful to start an interactive session on greatlakes, particularly for debugging. This is done from the terminal as follows:

```bash
module load python
srun --nodes=1 --account=stats_dept1 --ntasks-per-node=8 \
  --pty /bin/bash
```

- You can then run Python in the terminal by typing

```bash
python
```

- This Python session will have access to the cores you have requested.

- Here, we require `nodes=1` since `joblib` alone cannot work with cores across different machines. Multi-node computing requires tools such as `mpi4py` or `dask`.


---

- You can also run [Jupyter via the web-based Open OnDemand dashboard](https://greatlakes.arc-ts.umich.edu).
  However, your task here is to run batch jobs, which remain the basic tool for intensive statistical computing.
